metodos-de-estudio-que-de-verdad-funcion.titulo: Rereading and highlighting barely work: the review that evaluated 10 study techniques with real evidence
metodos-de-estudio-que-de-verdad-funcion.resumen: A comprehensive review of scientific evidence on study techniques found that self-testing (retrieval practice) and spacing out study sessions over time are the techniques with the highest proven utility, while rereading and highlighting, the most popular methods, yield poor results.

cuanto-tiempo-toma-formar-un-habito.titulo: How long does it actually take to form a healthy habit? (It's not 21 days)
cuanto-tiempo-toma-formar-un-habito.resumen: A meta-analysis of 20 studies involving 2,601 people found that health habits take an average of 59 to 154 days to form, with enormous variability from person to person, far from the popular "21 days" myth.

practica-deliberada-cuanto-explica-la-ex.titulo: Deliberate practice: how much skill mastery it actually explains, according to the meta-analysis that put Ericsson to the test
practica-deliberada-cuanto-explica-la-ex.resumen: A meta-analysis that re-analysed the evidence behind Anders Ericsson's deliberate practice theory found that the amount of practice explains a substantial portion of performance in games and music, but very little in professions and education, far from the "practice explains almost everything" idea popularised by the 10,000-hour rule.

mentalidad-de-crecimiento-que-dice-la-ev.titulo: "Growth mindset" is not magic: what a study of 12,000 students and two meta-analyses actually found
mentalidad-de-crecimiento-que-dice-la-ev.resumen: The idea that believing intelligence can be developed improves performance has real evidence behind it, but the effect is small and concentrated in certain students: it is not the universal solution often sold.

procrastinacion-productividad-estudianti.titulo: Almost all of us procrastinate: what really explains why we put things off and how it relates to performance
procrastinacion-productividad-estudianti.resumen: A meta-analysis of over 20 years of research found that procrastination is primarily explained by low self-efficacy and impulsivity, not by "laziness", and that it is consistently associated with lower academic performance.
